question: As we keep seeing in the news in Italy and beyond, juvenile delinquency is growing at a rapid rate. In recent years, there has been a significant increase in the number of criminal acts committed by very young people or ‘baby gangs’.

The link between youth violence and music is clear from recent reports, with trap artists, who society’s youngest members in particular idolise, becoming increasingly involved in often gang-related brawls, armed robberies and shootings. In view of the above, the EU Youth Strategy (framework for EU youth policy cooperation for 20192027) and the numerous incidents of violence taking place: 1.
Can the Commission say whether it considers the objectives to have been met?
What action will it take to limit record companies’ dissemination and promotion of violent music that negatively influences the behaviour of society’s youngest members?
answer: The EU Youth Strategy 2019-2027 (1) engages, connects, and empowers young people. It advances youth participation across policy areas and encourages young people to engage in respectful, tolerant, and non-violent dialogue, online and offline. The strategy does not deal directly with youth violence or criminal behaviour.

An assessment of the strategy and the degree to which it reaches its objectives is available in the Commission Report on the Interim evaluation of the EU Youth Strategy 20192027 (2), adopted in April 2024. In addition, the EU strategy on the rights of the child (3) is committed to fight any form of discrimination and combat violence against children.

The Commission also adopted an initiative on integrated child protection systems (4) to encourage national authorities to set up systemic solutions to tackle violence against children, online and offline.

It should be recalled that Article 6 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (5) provides that the EU has only a supportive, coordinating, or supplementing competence in the field of culture, which also encompasses music. Restrictions on the dissemination and promotion of music, and the appraisal of its alleged violent nature fall therefore outside the scope of the EU competence.
